prompt: Many countries invest heavily in training doctors, engineers and other skilled professionals, only for large numbers of them to emigrate soon after qualifying. Why does this happen, and what measures could reduce it?
essay:
Emigration by newly qualified professionals is usually framed as a loss of loyalty, and the measures that follow from that framing — bonds, exit restrictions, appeals to patriotism — have a poor record. They fail because they treat the departure as the problem, when it is more useful to treat it as a measurement. People with portable qualifications leave when the difference between what they can do at home and what they can do elsewhere becomes large enough to outweigh everything that holds them in place, and that difference is the thing worth examining.

Pay is part of it, but not the decisive part, and this matters because pay is the part that cannot be fixed. No middle-income health service will ever match salaries in the wealthiest countries, so a strategy built on closing that gap is a strategy built on losing. The more revealing complaints concern the work itself: equipment that is missing, decisions taken by people with no clinical knowledge, promotion that follows seniority rather than ability. A surgeon who cannot operate because a sterilisation unit has been broken for months is not weighing a salary; they are watching a decade of training go to waste.

That reframing changes what is worth spending money on. Functioning equipment, adequate support staff and competent management are cheap relative to salary matching and they address the frustration that salary matching does not. Merit-based advancement costs almost nothing and removes one of the most commonly cited reasons for leaving.

There is a further and often overlooked benefit. Conditions poor enough to drive professionals abroad also drive the ones who remain out of the profession, into private practice or into administration. A country that improves those conditions is not only retaining the doctors who would have emigrated. It is retaining the far larger number who never intended to leave and were quietly giving up anyway.
title: When trained graduates leave the country that educated them
